categoryBlurb: Almost every great pasta comes down to three habits: salt the water like you mean it, save a mug of that starchy water before you drain, and finish the noodles in the pan with the sauce instead of pouring sauce on top. Learn those three things here and the rest of the chapter cooks itself.

recipes.title: Spaghetti alla Carbonara
recipes.blurb: Eggs, cured pork, sharp sheep's cheese and black pepper turned into a glossy sauce with nothing but heat control and pasta water. There is no cream in it, and once you feel how the emulsion comes together you will never need a recipe again.

items: 1 lb (450 g) spaghetti, rigatoni, or bucatini
4 qt (3.8 L) water
1 tbsp (18 g) fine sea salt, for the pasta water
6 oz (170 g) guanciale, rind removed, cut into 1/4 in (6 mm) thick batons
4 large egg yolks plus 1 whole large egg, at room temperature
3 oz (85 g) Pecorino Romano, finely grated (about 1 1/4 cups packed)
1 1/2 tsp (4 g) coarsely ground black pepper, plus more for serving
1/4 tsp kosher salt, only if your guanciale is mild

instructions.title: Set everything out first
instructions.text: Carbonara happens in about 90 seconds at the end, so nothing can be hunting for a grater at that point. Grate the 3 oz (85 g) Pecorino now, crack the eggs into a wide bowl, cut the guanciale, and set a heatproof mixing bowl and tongs by the stove. Take the eggs out of the fridge 20 minutes ahead if you can, because cold yolks hitting hot pasta seize much faster than room-temperature ones.

instructions.title: Salt the water properly
instructions.text: Bring 4 qt (3.8 L) of water to a rolling boil in a large pot and add 1 tbsp (18 g) fine sea salt — it should taste like a mild soup, not the sea, because Pecorino is already very salty. Under-salted water is the single most common reason homemade pasta tastes flat no matter how good the sauce is. Do not add oil to the water; it coats the noodles and stops sauce from clinging later.

instructions.title: Render the guanciale slowly
instructions.text: Put the guanciale into a cold 12 in (30 cm) skillet and set it over medium-low heat. Starting cold lets the fat melt out gradually instead of the meat searing shut and staying chewy. Cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the pieces are deep gold with a crisp edge and about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of clear fat has pooled in the pan. It should sizzle steadily and smell nutty, never smoke.

instructions.title: Toast the pepper in the fat
instructions.text: Turn the heat off, scoop the crisp guanciale onto a plate with a slotted spoon, and leave the fat in the pan. Stir 1 1/2 tsp (4 g) coarse black pepper into the warm fat and let it sit for 30 seconds — the residual heat blooms the oils in the pepper and makes it taste floral rather than dusty. Do not do this over a live flame or the pepper turns bitter in seconds.

instructions.title: Build the egg and cheese paste
instructions.text: In your mixing bowl, whisk the 4 yolks and 1 whole egg with the grated Pecorino and a good grind of pepper until you have a thick, sandy paste that barely moves — think wet cake batter. The whole egg gives the sauce enough body to coat, while the extra yolks give richness without any cream. If it looks like scrambled-egg liquid rather than paste, add another tablespoon of cheese.

instructions.title: Cook the pasta just under al dente
instructions.text: Drop the pasta into the boiling water and stir for the first 30 seconds so it does not clump. Cook it 1 minute less than the low end of the package time, usually 8-9 minutes for spaghetti, so it still has a firm white thread in the center when you bite it. It will finish cooking in the pan, and pasta that is already soft when it leaves the water turns to mush in the sauce.

instructions.title: Save the pasta water
instructions.text: About a minute before draining, dip a heatproof measuring cup into the pot and pull out 2 cups (480 ml) of the cloudy, starchy water. That starch is the emulsifier that binds fat and egg into a sauce — plain tap water will not do the same job. Set the cup right next to your bowl, because you will use it three separate times in the next two minutes.

instructions.title: Temper the eggs
instructions.text: Whisking the egg mixture constantly, drizzle in about 1/3 cup (80 ml) of the hot pasta water in a thin stream. The mixture will loosen from a paste into a pourable cream and warm up to roughly 120°F (49°C), which is the whole trick: you are raising the egg temperature gradually instead of shocking it. Skip this step and the eggs will scramble the instant they meet the pasta.

instructions.title: Combine off the heat
instructions.text: Drain the pasta, dump it straight into the skillet with the peppery fat, and toss hard for 20-30 seconds so every strand is coated and glossy. Now take the skillet completely off the burner, wait 20 seconds so the pan drops below a sizzle, then pour in the tempered egg mixture and toss continuously. The residual heat of the pasta and pan is more than enough to cook the sauce.

instructions.title: Toss until it turns to silk
instructions.text: Keep the pasta moving with tongs for 45-60 seconds, adding pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until the sauce clings and slides off a strand in a smooth sheet rather than pooling at the bottom. If it seizes or looks grainy, the pan was too hot — pull it off, add a splash of cool pasta water, and keep tossing to bring it back. Finished carbonara should look like melted vanilla ice cream, not scrambled eggs.

instructions.title: Fold in the pork and serve
instructions.text: Stir in most of the crisped guanciale, saving a spoonful for the top, then taste for salt — with Pecorino this salty you usually need none, but if your guanciale was mild stir in the 1/4 tsp kosher salt now. Serve straight from the pan into warm bowls, because carbonara stiffens fast as it cools. Finish each bowl with the reserved guanciale, a little more Pecorino, and a heavy crack of black pepper.

tips: Guanciale is cured pork jowl and it is worth seeking out; pancetta is the next best thing, and thick-cut bacon works but brings smoke that is not traditional.
If the pan is even slightly too hot when the eggs go in, you get scrambled eggs. When in doubt, wait ten more seconds off the heat — the pasta holds plenty of heat.
Warm your serving bowls with hot tap water and dry them. Cold bowls drop the sauce temperature fast and it goes from silky to pasty in under a minute.
Carbonara does not reheat. If you must, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and warm it gently in a skillet while stirring, and accept that it will never be as good as it was at minute one.
No Pecorino? Use half Parmigiano-Reggiano and half Pecorino for a mellower sauce, and add a pinch more salt since Parmigiano is less salty.
recipes.keyTemp: The sauce should thicken at about 160°F (71°C) — hot enough to be safe and creamy, and well below the 180°F (82°C) where egg proteins clump and scramble.
recipes.pairing: A crisp Frascati or any dry Italian white, and a simple green salad with lemon to cut the richness.

recipes.title: Cacio e Pepe
recipes.blurb: Three ingredients, no cream, no butter — just cheese, pepper and starchy water whipped into a sauce that clings to every strand. It is the best thing you can make from an almost empty fridge, and it teaches you more about pasta water than any other dish.

items: 8 oz (225 g) tonnarelli, spaghetti, or bucatini
2 qt (1.9 L) water (deliberately less than usual, for starchier water)
1 1/2 tsp (9 g) fine sea salt, for the pasta water
4 oz (115 g) Pecorino Romano, grated on the fine side of a box grater (about 1 3/4 cups)
2 tsp (5 g) whole black peppercorns, coarsely cracked
1 tsp (5 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, for the pan

instructions.title: Grate the cheese very fine
instructions.text: Use the smallest holes on a box grater or a rasp grater so the Pecorino turns into a fluffy powder rather than shreds. Fine cheese melts into the water instantly; coarse shreds sink, clump, and turn into a stringy knot at the bottom of the pan. Grate all 4 oz (115 g) before you start cooking and keep it at room temperature.

instructions.title: Crack the peppercorns yourself
instructions.text: Put 2 tsp (5 g) whole peppercorns in a zip bag and crush them with the bottom of a heavy pan, or use the coarsest setting on a grinder. You want cracked, uneven pieces about the size of coarse sand, not fine dust. Pre-ground pepper has already lost the volatile oils that make this dish smell like a Roman trattoria.

instructions.title: Use less water on purpose
instructions.text: Bring just 2 qt (1.9 L) of water to a boil with 1 1/2 tsp (9 g) salt — about half what most people put on for a pot of pasta, and barely enough to cover 8 oz of spaghetti once it softens. Less water means the starch that leaches out of the noodles is far more concentrated, and that starch is the only thing standing between you and a broken, greasy sauce. Use a narrow saucepan rather than a stockpot so the strands stay submerged, and stir a little more often than usual since crowded pasta likes to stick. Salt lightly here because Pecorino brings a lot of salt of its own.

instructions.title: Toast the pepper
instructions.text: Set a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium heat, add the 1 tsp (5 ml) olive oil and the cracked pepper, and swirl for 45-60 seconds until it smells sharp and perfumed. It should sizzle faintly at the edges, never smoke. Toasting wakes up the piperine and gives the finished dish a warm heat instead of a dry scratch at the back of the throat.

instructions.title: Cook the pasta short
instructions.text: Add the pasta to the boiling water and stir well for the first 30 seconds. Cook it 2 minutes shy of the package time — around 7 minutes for dried spaghetti — so it is distinctly chewy. It finishes in the pan, and this shortfall is what lets the noodles absorb the peppery liquid instead of just sitting in it.

instructions.title: Pull a full mug of pasta water
instructions.text: Before draining, ladle out 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of the cloudy water — take it from deep in the pot, where the starch is thickest. It should look faintly milky, almost like watered-down skim milk; that is the visual cue that you have enough dissolved starch to build a sauce. Because you started with only 2 qt, this water is roughly twice as starchy as normal pasta water, which is exactly the point. Set it beside the stove, because you will use most of it in the next two minutes.

instructions.title: Make the cheese slurry
instructions.text: In a small bowl, whisk about half the grated Pecorino with 1/3 cup (80 ml) of the hot pasta water until you have a smooth, loose paste with no lumps, roughly the texture of pancake batter. This pre-melting step is the safety net that stops the cheese from hitting a hot pan and instantly balling up. If it looks stringy, whisk in another tablespoon of water.

instructions.title: Move the pasta into the pan
instructions.text: Lift the pasta directly from the pot into the skillet with tongs, letting the water that clings to it come along, and add another 1/2 cup (120 ml) of pasta water. Turn the heat to medium and toss constantly for about 1 minute as the liquid bubbles and reduces around the noodles. The pasta should finish cooking here, drinking in the pepper as it goes.

instructions.title: Kill the heat, then add cheese
instructions.text: Take the skillet fully off the burner and let it cool for about 20 seconds — you should be able to hold your hand an inch above it without flinching. Pour in the cheese slurry and toss hard and continuously, adding the remaining cheese in two handfuls. Direct heat above roughly 170°F (77°C) makes Pecorino split into rubber and oil, so the pan must be off the flame.

instructions.title: Whip it into a sauce
instructions.text: Keep tossing and stirring vigorously for 30-60 seconds, splashing in pasta water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time until the sauce turns creamy and coats the strands with a visible sheen. If it clumps, add a little more hot water and keep working it — most broken cacio e pepe can be rescued with water and motion. Serve immediately in warmed bowls with extra pepper on top.

tips: The number one failure is heat. If you can hear an aggressive sizzle when the cheese goes in, it is too hot and it will seize.
A splash of cold pasta water can shock a clumping sauce back together — keep 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the reserved water cooling on the counter as insurance.
For a slightly more forgiving version, use 3 oz (85 g) Pecorino plus 1 oz (30 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano; the Parmigiano melts more smoothly.
Tonnarelli or spaghetti alla chitarra are traditional because their rough square edges hold the sauce, but any bronze-die dried pasta works better than a slick supermarket brand.
Cook this for two at most. Scaling past 1 lb (450 g) of pasta makes the emulsion much harder to control in a single pan.
recipes.keyTemp: Add the cheese only once the pan is off the heat and below about 170°F (77°C); above that Pecorino breaks into oily strings instead of melting into cream.
recipes.pairing: A cold, dry white like Vermentino, and nothing else on the table — this dish deserves to be the whole meal.

recipes.title: Spaghetti Aglio e Olio
recipes.blurb: Garlic gently toasted in good olive oil, chili, parsley and a splash of pasta water — dinner from a bare pantry in twenty minutes. Make it once at midnight and it becomes a permanent part of your life.

items: 1 lb (450 g) spaghetti or linguine
4 qt (3.8 L) water
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water
1/2 cup (120 ml) good extra-virgin olive oil, plus 1 tbsp (15 ml) for finishing
8 large garlic cloves (about 1 1/2 oz / 40 g), thinly sliced
3/4 tsp red pepper flakes, or up to 1 1/2 tsp if you like heat
1/2 cup (20 g) fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped
1 tbsp (15 ml) fresh lemon juice
1/2 cup (40 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano, optional

instructions.title: Slice the garlic thin and even
instructions.text: Trim the root end off each clove and slice lengthwise about 1/16 in (2 mm) thick — thin enough to see light through, but not paper-shaved. Even slices brown at the same rate, and uneven ones mean some pieces are still raw while others have gone bitter and black. A small paring knife gives you far more control here than a chef's knife.

instructions.title: Get the water going
instructions.text: Bring 4 qt (3.8 L) of water to a rolling boil and add 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt. This is the dish where properly salted water matters most, because there is no cheese, cream, or meat to carry seasoning. Taste it — it should taste distinctly seasoned, like a good broth.

instructions.title: Start the garlic cold
instructions.text: Pour the 1/2 cup (120 ml) olive oil into a cold 12 in (30 cm) skillet, add the sliced garlic, and only then turn the heat to medium-low. Starting in cold oil lets the garlic release its flavor slowly over 5-7 minutes instead of scorching in 30 seconds. You are looking for a lazy, steady bubbling around the slices, not a hard fry.

instructions.title: Take it to pale gold, no further
instructions.text: Stir occasionally and watch closely; pull the pan off the heat the moment the slices turn the color of light straw, around 6-8 minutes in. Garlic carries residual heat and keeps darkening in the oil after the burner is off, so stopping early is the right call. Burnt garlic is acrid and there is no fixing it — if it goes dark brown, wipe the pan and start over.

instructions.title: Bloom the chili
instructions.text: With the pan off the heat, stir in the 3/4 tsp red pepper flakes and let them sit in the warm oil for 30 seconds. The heat draws the capsaicin and the red color out into the oil, which is what turns this from spicy specks into a sauce with an even warm glow. Add more flakes now if you want a real kick.

instructions.title: Cook the pasta al dente
instructions.text: Drop the spaghetti into the boiling water, stir for the first 30 seconds, then cook 1 minute less than the package says — usually 8 minutes. Bite a strand: there should be a thin, firm white core. That last minute of cooking happens in the oil, where the noodle drinks up garlic instead of plain water.

instructions.title: Reserve the starchy water
instructions.text: Scoop out 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of pasta water before draining, using a heatproof mug or measuring cup dipped straight into the pot. In a dish that is essentially oil and water, this starch is the only thing that will hold the two together into a sauce instead of a slick. Reserve more than you think you need — the single most common mistake here is draining the pot and realizing the water is gone. Keep the cup hot right next to the stove so you are not adding cold liquid to a hot pan.

instructions.title: Marry pasta and oil
instructions.text: Return the skillet to medium heat, add the drained pasta along with 3/4 cup (180 ml) of the reserved water, and toss with tongs for 1-2 minutes. The liquid will bubble hard and start to thicken as the starch does its work. Keep the pasta moving so every strand passes through the oil.

instructions.title: Emulsify and finish
instructions.text: Toss vigorously, adding more pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until the sauce looks slightly cloudy and clings to the noodles rather than sliding to the bottom of the pan. Off the heat, stir in the parsley, the 1 tbsp (15 ml) lemon juice, and the Parmigiano if using. Taste and add a pinch more salt or chili.

instructions.title: Serve right away
instructions.text: Divide among four warmed bowls and finish each with a thin drizzle of the reserved 1 tbsp (15 ml) raw olive oil for aroma. This dish waits for no one — the emulsion tightens within a few minutes and the parsley loses its brightness. Eat it standing up in the kitchen if you have to.

tips: Use the best olive oil you own. With four ingredients, the oil is the flavor, and a peppery unfiltered extra-virgin makes a noticeable difference.
For a version closer to what you get in Naples, toast 1/2 cup (25 g) panko in 1 tbsp oil until golden and scatter it over the top for crunch.
Anchovies are not traditional but 3 fillets melted into the oil with the garlic add savory depth without tasting fishy.
If your garlic browns too fast, your heat is too high. Medium-low is not a suggestion — the whole point is a slow infusion.
recipes.keyTemp: No internal temperature applies; the garlic is the gauge — pale straw gold and fragrant, pulled off the heat before it reaches brown. The oil should stay around 250-275°F (120-135°C), gently bubbling.
recipes.pairing: A cold glass of Falanghina or a light beer, with crusty bread to mop the garlicky oil from the bowl.

recipes.title: Tagliatelle with Ragu alla Bolognese
recipes.blurb: The real thing from Emilia-Romagna: mostly meat, barely any tomato, finished with milk, and simmered for hours until it turns velvety and dark. It is a Sunday project that fills the apartment with the best smell there is.

items: 1 medium yellow onion (8 oz / 225 g), finely diced
1 large carrot (4 oz / 115 g), finely diced
2 celery ribs (4 oz / 115 g), finely diced
3 tbsp (42 g) unsalted butter
2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil
4 oz (115 g) pancetta, finely chopped
1 lb (450 g) ground beef chuck (80/20)
8 oz (225 g) ground pork
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1 cup (240 ml) dry white wine
1 cup (240 ml) whole milk
3 tbsp (50 g) tomato paste
1 (14.5 oz / 411 g) can whole peeled tomatoes, crushed by hand
2 cups (480 ml) low-sodium beef or chicken stock, plus more as needed
1/8 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
1 lb (450 g) fresh egg tagliatelle, or 1 lb (450 g) dried tagliatelle or pappardelle
2 tbsp (28 g) unsalted butter, cold
3 oz (85 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated, plus more at the table
5 qt (4.7 L) water, for the pasta
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water

instructions.title: Cut the soffritto very fine
instructions.text: Dice the onion, carrot and celery into pieces no bigger than 1/8 in (3 mm) — smaller than feels necessary. Over three hours these vegetables should melt away completely and become invisible body in the sauce, not chunks you bite into. A food processor pulsed 8-10 times works, but drain off any liquid it releases so the soffritto can brown.

instructions.title: Sweat the vegetables
instructions.text: In a heavy 6-8 qt (6-8 L) Dutch oven, melt the 3 tbsp butter with the 2 tbsp olive oil over medium heat, then add the soffritto with a pinch of salt. Cook for 10-12 minutes, stirring often, until everything is soft and the onion is translucent and just starting to take on color at the edges. It should sigh and sizzle gently, never brown hard — you want sweetness, not roast.

instructions.title: Render the pancetta
instructions.text: Add the chopped pancetta and cook another 5 minutes until its fat has rendered out and the pieces are lightly golden. This is the savory backbone of the sauce and it needs its own moment before the ground meat arrives. The pan will look a little greasy and that is exactly right.

instructions.title: Brown the meat in stages
instructions.text: Raise the heat to medium-high and add the beef and pork in two batches, breaking each up with a wooden spoon and letting it sit undisturbed for 2-3 minutes before stirring. Season with the 1 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper. Crowding all the meat in at once drops the pan temperature and it steams grey instead of browning, which costs you the deep flavor that makes this sauce taste like more than the sum of its parts.

instructions.title: Deglaze with white wine
instructions.text: Pour in the 1 cup (240 ml) white wine and scrape the bottom of the pot hard with a wooden spoon to lift every browned bit. Simmer for 4-6 minutes until the sharp alcohol smell is gone and the liquid has reduced by about half. White wine, not red, is traditional here — it keeps the sauce bright rather than heavy.

instructions.title: Add the milk and let it disappear
instructions.text: Pour in the 1 cup (240 ml) whole milk and lower the heat to medium. Simmer gently for 10-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the milk is almost fully absorbed and the surface looks glossy. Milk tenderizes the meat proteins and rounds out the acidity of the wine and tomato — do not skip it, and do not panic if it looks curdled at first, because it smooths out as it cooks down.

instructions.title: Build the tomato base
instructions.text: Stir in the 3 tbsp tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes until it darkens from bright red to brick and smells sweet rather than tinny. Add the hand-crushed canned tomatoes with their juice, the 2 cups (480 ml) stock, and the nutmeg. Bolognese is a meat sauce with tomato in it, not a tomato sauce with meat — this restraint is what makes it taste different from what most people call bolognese.

instructions.title: Simmer low for three hours
instructions.text: Bring the pot to a bare simmer, then drop the heat as low as it will go, leaving the lid slightly ajar. You want one lazy bubble breaking the surface every couple of seconds, roughly 195°F (91°C). Cook for 2 1/2 to 3 hours, stirring every 20-30 minutes and adding 1/2 cup (120 ml) of stock or water any time the surface looks dry.

instructions.title: Know when it is done
instructions.text: The ragu is ready when the fat has separated into orange pools at the edges, the color has gone from red to a deep russet brown, and a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a track that fills in slowly. The meat should feel soft enough to crush against the roof of your mouth. Taste and adjust salt now, because a long-simmered sauce needs more than you would expect.

instructions.title: Boil the tagliatelle
instructions.text: Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt. Fresh tagliatelle needs only 2-3 minutes and floats when it is close; dried needs 1 minute less than the package time. Reserve 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of pasta water before you drain.

instructions.title: Finish the pasta in the sauce
instructions.text: Ladle about 3 cups (700 ml) of ragu into a wide skillet over medium heat, add the drained pasta and 1/2 cup (120 ml) pasta water, and toss for 1-2 minutes so the noodles absorb the sauce instead of wearing it. Kill the heat, add the 2 tbsp cold butter and the grated Parmigiano, and toss until glossy. Add more pasta water a splash at a time if it looks tight.

instructions.title: Serve and stash the rest
instructions.text: Serve in warm bowls with extra Parmigiano and no basil, no garlic bread, no fuss. You will have 2-3 cups of ragu left over, which is the whole point. It keeps 4 days in the fridge and 3 months frozen, and it is even better on day two.

tips: Make the ragu a day ahead. Overnight in the fridge the flavors settle and deepen, and you can lift off any excess fat from the top before reheating.
Tagliatelle exists because flat, porous egg noodles hold a meat sauce. Spaghetti is genuinely the wrong shape here — it sheds the ragu into the bottom of the bowl.
If the sauce tastes sharp or thin at the two-hour mark, it needs more time, not more salt. Long simmering is what converts acidity into sweetness.
Freeze leftovers flat in 2-cup portions in zip bags. They thaw in 20 minutes in a bowl of warm water and turn a Tuesday into something good.
No white wine? Use dry vermouth, or skip it and add 1 extra cup of stock plus 1 tsp red wine vinegar at the end for lift.
recipes.keyTemp: Ground beef and pork are safe at 160°F (71°C); a proper ragu holds near 195°F (91°C) for hours, so you are cooking well past safety and purely for texture.
recipes.pairing: A bottle of Sangiovese or Lambrusco, and a plain arugula salad with lemon and olive oil afterward.

recipes.title: Fettuccine Alfredo from Scratch
recipes.blurb: The original Roman version: butter, real Parmigiano, and pasta water beaten into a sauce so rich it seems like there must be cream in it. There isn't, and that is exactly why it tastes so clean.

items: 12 oz (340 g) fresh or dried fettuccine
4 qt (3.8 L) water
1 tbsp (18 g) fine sea salt, for the pasta water
6 tbsp (85 g) high-fat unsalted butter, cut into 6 pieces and softened
5 oz (140 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, grated on a rasp until powdery (about 2 1/2 cups)
1/2 tsp freshly ground white or black pepper
1/8 tsp freshly grated nutmeg, optional

instructions.title: Bring the butter and cheese to room temperature
instructions.text: Set the 6 tbsp (85 g) butter on the counter for 30 minutes and grate the Parmigiano just before cooking. Cold butter and cold cheese hitting hot pasta is the fastest route to a broken, greasy sauce. The butter should dent easily when you press it but still hold its shape.

instructions.title: Grate the cheese to a powder
instructions.text: Use a rasp grater, not the box grater's shredding holes — you want the Parmigiano to look like fine snow. Powdered cheese dissolves into the water and butter almost instantly, while shreds clump and string. This single detail is the difference between silk and glue.

instructions.title: Warm the serving bowl
instructions.text: Fill a large, wide serving bowl with hot tap water and let it sit while the pasta water heats, then dump it out and dry the bowl right before you use it. Traditional Alfredo is tossed in a warm bowl, not a hot pan, because direct flame is what causes the cheese to split. A warm bowl keeps everything fluid without cooking it.

instructions.title: Salt the water lightly
instructions.text: Bring 4 qt (3.8 L) of water to a boil and add just 1 tbsp (18 g) fine sea salt — less than usual, because 5 oz of Parmigiano brings plenty of salt. Give the water a taste; it should be mildly seasoned, not aggressive. Over-salting here makes the finished dish taste harsh.

instructions.title: Cook the fettuccine
instructions.text: Add the pasta and stir for the first 30 seconds so the strands do not fuse. Fresh fettuccine takes 2-3 minutes and is done when it floats and the edges look tender; dried takes about 1 minute less than the package time. It should still be firm because the tossing at the end finishes it.

instructions.title: Reserve plenty of water
instructions.text: Scoop out 2 cups (480 ml) of the starchy cooking water before draining. This sauce is built almost entirely on that water, so having too much is far better than running short. The water should look cloudy — if it looks clear, your ratio of water to pasta was too high.

instructions.title: Start the emulsion in the bowl
instructions.text: Put the softened butter in the warmed bowl with 1/2 cup (120 ml) of hot pasta water and whisk until the butter melts into a cloudy, unified liquid. You are building a butter-and-water emulsion first, before any cheese enters the picture. If it looks like melted butter floating on water, keep whisking — it will come together.

instructions.title: Add the pasta hot
instructions.text: Lift the fettuccine straight from the pot into the bowl with tongs, dripping wet, and toss immediately so every strand is coated in the buttery liquid. Work fast and keep the pasta moving; this is where the noodle's own surface starch joins the party. Add a splash more pasta water if it starts looking dry.

instructions.title: Fold in the cheese in stages
instructions.text: Add the Parmigiano in three handfuls, tossing hard with tongs after each one and adding 2-3 tbsp (30-45 ml) of pasta water between additions. Doing it gradually keeps the cheese suspended instead of dropping into a lump. After the last handful the sauce should turn pale ivory and start visibly clinging to the strands.

instructions.title: Beat it until glossy
instructions.text: Toss and lift the pasta for a full 60-90 seconds, which feels like a long time but is what whips the sauce into that famous glossy cream. Add pasta water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time until the sauce ribbons off a strand rather than clinging in clumps. Season with the pepper and nutmeg if using, then serve immediately — Alfredo waits about four minutes before it stiffens.

tips: Use real Parmigiano-Reggiano with the pin-dot lettering on the rind. Pre-grated cheese is coated with cellulose to prevent caking and it will refuse to emulsify.
If the sauce breaks and turns oily, take it off any heat, add 1/4 cup (60 ml) hot pasta water, and beat hard with a whisk — most breaks come back.
For an American-style Alfredo, warm 1 cup (240 ml) heavy cream with the butter and reduce by a third before adding cheese. It is far more forgiving and holds better for leftovers.
Grilled chicken or seared shrimp turn this into a full meal; cook them separately and lay them on top so their juices do not thin the sauce.
Never make Alfredo ahead. The emulsion is temporary by design and reheated Alfredo separates into butter and grit.
recipes.keyTemp: There is no internal temperature — the cue is visual. Keep the mixture below about 175°F (79°C) so the Parmigiano stays emulsified, and stop when the sauce coats a strand in a glossy, unbroken sheet.
recipes.pairing: A crisp Pinot Grigio or Chardonnay and a bitter salad of radicchio and endive to cut through all that butter.

recipes.title: Baked Ziti with Sausage and Ricotta
recipes.blurb: Layers of tubey pasta, quick sausage tomato sauce, dollops of ricotta and a lid of browned mozzarella. It is the easiest big-pan dinner in the book and it feeds a crowd or a whole week of lunches.

items: 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil
1 lb (450 g) bulk Italian sausage, sweet or hot, casings removed
1 medium yellow onion (8 oz / 225 g), finely chopped
4 garlic cloves, minced
1 tsp (1 g) dried oregano
1/2 tsp red pepper flakes
1 (28 oz / 794 g) can crushed tomatoes
1 (15 oz / 425 g) can tomato sauce
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/2 cup (20 g) fresh basil leaves, torn
1 lb (450 g) ziti or penne rigate
5 qt (4.7 L) water, for the pasta
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water
15 oz (425 g) whole-milk ricotta
1 large egg
3 oz (85 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated, plus more for serving
12 oz (340 g) low-moisture whole-milk mozzarella, shredded
1/4 cup (10 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1/2 tsp kosher salt and 1/4 tsp freshly ground black pepper, for the ricotta filling

instructions.title: Heat the oven and pan
instructions.text: Set an oven rack in the upper third and heat the oven to 375°F (190°C), giving it a full 15 minutes to come up to temperature before anything goes in. Lightly oil a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish, getting into the corners so the edges release cleanly later. Putting the rack high means the cheese on top browns properly instead of just melting into a pale blanket, because the heating element radiates down onto it. Start the oven now and it will be ready by the time the sauce has simmered.

instructions.title: Brown the sausage hard
instructions.text: Heat the 2 tbsp olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high, add the sausage, and press it into a flat layer. Let it sit untouched for 4-5 minutes so a deep brown crust forms, then break it into rough 1/2 in (1 cm) chunks and cook 3 minutes more. Those browned bits are the difference between a sauce that tastes like tomatoes and one that tastes like dinner.

instructions.title: Soften the aromatics
instructions.text: Lower the heat to medium and add the chopped onion with a pinch of salt, cooking 5-6 minutes until soft and translucent. Stir in the garlic, oregano, and red pepper flakes and cook just 45 seconds, until the garlic smells sweet. Garlic burns in about a minute at this temperature, so keep it moving.

instructions.title: Simmer the sauce
instructions.text: Pour in the crushed tomatoes and tomato sauce, add the 1 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper, and bring to a gentle bubble. Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens enough that a spoon leaves a brief trail. Stir in the torn basil at the very end so it stays fresh and green.

instructions.title: Boil the pasta very short
instructions.text: While the sauce simmers, bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and cook the ziti for only 6-7 minutes — a full 3 minutes less than the package time. It will feel unpleasantly firm and that is correct. The pasta absorbs sauce and finishes cooking in the oven, and fully cooked pasta going into a baking dish comes out mushy every single time.

instructions.title: Save pasta water and drain
instructions.text: Reserve 1 cup (240 ml) of the starchy water before draining, then drain the ziti and immediately toss it with about 1 cup (240 ml) of the sauce so it does not stick together. That coating of sauce also seals the surface starch so the noodles stay distinct. Do not rinse the pasta — you would wash away the starch that helps everything bind.

instructions.title: Mix the ricotta filling
instructions.text: In a bowl, stir the 15 oz (425 g) ricotta with the egg, two-thirds of the grated Parmigiano and the parsley, then season with the 1/2 tsp kosher salt and 1/4 tsp black pepper reserved for the filling. Mix until it is smooth and uniform, but stop there — overworking ricotta thins it out. The egg is what sets the filling into creamy pockets instead of letting it go grainy and watery in the oven, so do not leave it out. If your ricotta looks wet or has whey pooled on top, drain it in a sieve for 10 minutes first.

instructions.title: Combine pasta and sauce
instructions.text: Add the remaining sauce and about 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the reserved pasta water to the pasta and fold until every tube is coated inside and out. It should look a little looser than you think it needs to be, since the pasta will keep drinking liquid in the oven. Fold in half the shredded mozzarella.

instructions.title: Layer the dish
instructions.text: Spread half the pasta in the baking dish, dollop the ricotta mixture over it in tablespoon-sized spoonfuls, then top with the remaining pasta. Dollops beat a smooth layer here because you get distinct creamy pockets rather than one dense stratum. Press the top down lightly so everything settles.

instructions.title: Top and bake covered
instructions.text: Scatter the remaining mozzarella and Parmigiano over the top, cover tightly with foil, and bake for 25 minutes. Covering traps steam so the pasta hydrates fully and the middle heats through before the top sets. Tent the foil slightly so it does not stick to the cheese.

instructions.title: Uncover and brown
instructions.text: Remove the foil and bake another 15-20 minutes until the cheese is bubbling across the whole surface with brown freckles at the edges and the center reaches 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer. If it is hot but pale, run it under the broiler for 2 minutes, watching constantly. Broilers go from golden to burnt in about 45 seconds.

instructions.title: Rest before serving
instructions.text: Let the dish sit on the counter for 10-15 minutes before cutting. The molten cheese and sauce need that time to set enough to hold a square shape on the plate. Cut into 8 pieces with a sharp knife and serve with extra Parmigiano.

tips: Assemble it up to 2 days ahead, cover, and refrigerate unbaked. Add 15 minutes to the covered bake time and start it straight from cold.
To freeze, assemble in a foil pan, wrap in plastic then foil, and freeze up to 3 months. Bake from frozen at 375°F (190°C) covered for 75 minutes, then uncovered for 20.
Shred your own mozzarella from a block. Pre-shredded is coated in starch and bakes up rubbery and oily.
Ziti, penne rigate and rigatoni all work because their ridges and hollows trap sauce; smooth penne lisce slides right out of it.
For a vegetarian version, swap the sausage for 1 lb (450 g) of cremini mushrooms browned hard in two batches, plus 1 tsp fennel seed for that sausage note.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake until the center registers 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer and the sauce is bubbling at the edges; cooked sausage is safe at 160°F (71°C).
recipes.pairing: A simple Chianti and a Caesar or a big garlicky green salad — this dish needs something sharp beside it.

recipes.title: Lasagna alla Bolognese
recipes.blurb: The northern Italian original — slow ragu, silky bechamel, thin sheets of pasta, and Parmigiano instead of a pound of mozzarella. It takes an afternoon, and it is the single most impressive thing you can put on a table.

items: 3 tbsp (42 g) unsalted butter plus 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil
1 onion (8 oz / 225 g), 1 carrot (4 oz / 115 g) and 2 celery ribs (4 oz / 115 g), all finely diced
4 oz (115 g) pancetta, finely chopped
1 lb (450 g) ground beef chuck (80/20) and 8 oz (225 g) ground pork
1 cup (240 ml) dry white wine
1 cup (240 ml) whole milk
3 tbsp (50 g) tomato paste and 1 (14.5 oz / 411 g) can whole peeled tomatoes, crushed
2 cups (480 ml) beef or chicken stock
2 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp black pepper
4 tbsp (57 g) unsalted butter
1/2 cup (60 g) all-purpose flour
4 cups (960 ml) whole milk, warmed
1 1/4 tsp kosher salt
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
1/4 tsp white pepper
1 lb (450 g) fresh egg lasagna sheets, or 12 oz (340 g) dried flat lasagna noodles
8 oz (225 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated
3 tbsp (42 g) unsalted butter — 1 tbsp softened for the dish, 2 tbsp cut into small bits for the top
6 qt (5.7 L) water, for blanching the pasta
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for blanching the pasta

instructions.title: Start the ragu
instructions.text: Melt the 3 tbsp butter with the 2 tbsp olive oil in a heavy 6 qt (6 L) Dutch oven over medium heat and cook the finely diced onion, carrot and celery for 10-12 minutes until soft and barely golden. Add the pancetta and cook 5 minutes more until its fat renders and the bits turn light gold. Take your time here; this base carries the whole dish.

instructions.title: Brown the meat in batches
instructions.text: Raise the heat to medium-high and add half the beef and pork, spreading it flat and letting it sit for 3 minutes before breaking it up. Repeat with the second batch and season with the 2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper. If you dump all 1 1/2 lb in at once the pot floods with liquid and the meat boils grey instead of browning.

instructions.title: Wine, then milk, then tomato
instructions.text: Add the 1 cup (240 ml) white wine and scrape the bottom clean, simmering 5 minutes until the raw alcohol smell disappears. Stir in the 1 cup (240 ml) milk and cook 12-15 minutes until it is nearly absorbed and the surface looks glossy. Then add the tomato paste, cook it 2 minutes until brick-colored, and add the crushed tomatoes and 2 cups (480 ml) stock.

instructions.title: Simmer for three hours
instructions.text: Drop the heat to the lowest setting, set the lid ajar, and let the ragu simmer at about 195°F (91°C) for 2 1/2 to 3 hours. Stir every half hour and add 1/2 cup (120 ml) water whenever it looks dry. It is finished when the color is deep russet, the fat has separated into orange pools, and the meat crushes easily against the side of the pot.

instructions.title: Make the besciamella
instructions.text: Melt the 4 tbsp (57 g) butter in a 3 qt (3 L) saucepan over medium heat, whisk in the 1/2 cup (60 g) flour, and cook 2 minutes until it smells faintly like toasted popcorn but is still pale. Equal weights of butter and flour is the ratio that actually sets — a besciamella built on less flour stays runny and your layers will slide apart when you cut the lasagna. Pour in the warm milk in three additions, whisking hard after each until completely smooth before the next goes in. Bring it to a bare simmer and cook 6-8 minutes until it thickly coats the back of a spoon, then season with the salt, nutmeg and white pepper.

instructions.title: Keep the sauce from skinning
instructions.text: Press a piece of plastic wrap directly onto the surface of the besciamella, touching the sauce all over. A skin forms within minutes on exposed hot dairy and it turns into rubbery flecks in the finished lasagna. It should be the consistency of thin pancake batter, loose enough to spread with the back of a spoon.

instructions.title: Blanch the pasta sheets
instructions.text: Bring 6 qt (5.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and set a bowl of ice water beside it. Boil fresh sheets 45-60 seconds or dried sheets 4 minutes, then transfer them to the ice water for 30 seconds and lay them flat on clean kitchen towels. Under-cooking here is deliberate; the sheets finish in the oven and over-boiled pasta tears the moment you touch it.

instructions.title: Heat the oven and prep the pan
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the middle and grease a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish with the 1 tbsp softened butter, working it up the sides as well as across the base. Spread a thin layer of besciamella over that, about 1/2 cup (120 ml), just enough to film the bottom. That slick of fat and sauce keeps the first pasta layer from gluing itself to the dish, which is what tears the bottom sheet when you try to serve. Do this before you start layering, because once your hands are covered in ragu you will not want to stop.

instructions.title: Layer it properly
instructions.text: Build six layers in this order every time: pasta, about 3/4 cup (180 ml) ragu spread thin, about 1/2 cup (120 ml) besciamella, then a generous scatter of Parmigiano. Trim the sheets to fit rather than overlapping them much, since doubled-up pasta stays gummy. Traditional bolognese lasagna is thin-layered and restrained, not overstuffed.

instructions.title: Finish the top
instructions.text: End with a layer of pasta, the last of the besciamella spread all the way to the corners, a heavy shower of Parmigiano, and the 2 tbsp of butter bits dotted over the surface. Those butter dots are what give the top its blistered golden lace. Make sure no pasta is left exposed or it will dry into shards.

instructions.title: Bake covered, then uncovered
instructions.text: Cover with foil tented so it does not touch the cheese and bake for 30 minutes, then remove the foil and bake 20-25 minutes more. It is ready when the top is deeply golden with crisp brown edges and the center reads 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer. You should see the sauce bubbling slowly around the perimeter.

instructions.title: Rest a full thirty minutes
instructions.text: Move the lasagna to a rack and leave it alone for 30 minutes — this is not optional. Straight out of the oven the layers are liquid and a slice will slump into a puddle, while a rested lasagna cuts into clean squares that hold their stripes. It will still be hot at the center after half an hour.

tips: Split the work over two days: ragu and besciamella on Saturday, assemble and bake on Sunday. The ragu is genuinely better after a night in the fridge.
Fresh spinach lasagna sheets are what they use in Bologna and they are worth buying if your grocery store carries them. Skip the no-boil sheets, which stay chalky under a thin-layered lasagna.
If your besciamella goes lumpy, blitz it with an immersion blender for 15 seconds and it will come back perfectly smooth.
No mozzarella belongs in a real lasagna bolognese. The stretchy cheese pull is an American addition and it makes the layers heavy and greasy.
Baked and cooled lasagna cuts even more neatly cold. Refrigerate overnight, cut into squares, and reheat individual portions at 350°F (175°C) for 20 minutes.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake until the center hits 165°F (74°C); the ground meat in the ragu passed its 160°F (71°C) safe point hours earlier during the simmer.
recipes.pairing: A structured Sangiovese such as Chianti Classico, and only a bitter green salad afterward — nothing else can compete.

recipes.title: Shrimp Scampi Linguine
recipes.blurb: Garlic, white wine, butter and lemon reduced into a glossy pan sauce with plump shrimp folded through. It comes together faster than the pasta boils, which makes it the best last-minute impressive dinner there is.

items: 1 lb (450 g) large shrimp (21/25 count), peeled and deveined, tails off
12 oz (340 g) linguine
5 qt (4.7 L) water, for the pasta
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water
1 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp black pepper, for the shrimp
3 tbsp (45 ml) olive oil
6 tbsp (85 g) unsalted butter, cut into 6 pieces and kept cold
6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1/2 tsp red pepper flakes
3/4 cup (180 ml) dry white wine such as Pinot Grigio
3 tbsp (45 ml) fresh lemon juice plus 1 tsp finely grated zest (about 2 lemons), plus 1 more lemon cut into wedges for serving
1/3 cup (13 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley

instructions.title: Dry and season the shrimp
instructions.text: Pat the shrimp completely dry with paper towels and toss with 1 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp black pepper. Wet shrimp steam in the pan and turn out pale and rubbery instead of picking up color. Leave them on the counter while you get the water going so they lose their refrigerator chill.

instructions.title: Start the pasta water
instructions.text: Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a rolling boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt. Time it so the pasta goes in right when you start cooking the shrimp — the whole dish takes about 12 minutes from that point. Have your reserved-water mug and a colander ready.

instructions.title: Sear the shrimp fast
instructions.text: Heat the 3 tbsp olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then lay the shrimp in a single layer without crowding, working in two batches if needed. Cook 60-75 seconds per side, just until the outsides turn opaque pink with a little browning and the centers are still slightly translucent. They will finish in the sauce, and shrimp go from tender to rubber in about 30 seconds of overcooking.

instructions.title: Get the shrimp out
instructions.text: Transfer the shrimp to a plate immediately — do not leave them in a hot pan while you do anything else. Residual pan heat keeps cooking them, and this pause is the main thing separating a good scampi from a chewy one. Pour any juices that collect on the plate back into the sauce later.

instructions.title: Drop the pasta
instructions.text: Add the linguine to the boiling water now and stir for the first 30 seconds. Cook it 2 minutes less than the package time, usually about 8 minutes, so it is firmly chewy. It will finish in the pan sauce, which is where it picks up all that garlic and wine.

instructions.title: Soften the garlic gently
instructions.text: Lower the skillet heat to medium, add the sliced garlic and 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes to the oil left in the pan, and cook 60-90 seconds, stirring constantly. Stop the moment the garlic turns pale gold and smells sweet. If the pan is still ripping hot from searing, pull it off the burner for 20 seconds first — garlic goes from fragrant to bitter faster than anything else in a kitchen.

instructions.title: Reduce the wine
instructions.text: Pour in the 3/4 cup (180 ml) white wine and scrape up any browned bits stuck to the pan. Simmer briskly for 3-4 minutes until the liquid has reduced by about half and the sharp alcohol edge is gone. What is left should smell rounded and slightly sweet, and coat the bottom of the pan in a shallow layer.

instructions.title: Reserve the pasta water
instructions.text: Scoop out 1 cup (240 ml) of the starchy pasta water before draining, dipping a heatproof mug straight into the pot. This is what will bind the butter into the wine so the sauce clings to the linguine instead of pooling at the bottom of the bowl. Starch molecules coat the fat droplets and hold them suspended in the liquid, which is the same trick behind every pan sauce in this chapter. Keep the mug hot right beside the pan, because cold water dropped into a butter sauce will break it.

instructions.title: Mount the butter
instructions.text: Turn the heat to low, add 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the pasta water, then drop in the cold butter one piece at a time, swirling the pan constantly so each piece melts before the next goes in. This gradual, low-heat swirl is what emulsifies butter into a creamy sauce rather than letting it separate into oil. Stir in the 3 tbsp lemon juice and the zest.

instructions.title: Finish the pasta in the sauce
instructions.text: Add the drained linguine directly to the skillet and toss with tongs over low heat for 1-2 minutes, adding pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until the sauce clings to the noodles. The pasta will absorb some of the liquid and thicken the whole thing as it does. Taste for salt and lemon now, before the shrimp go back in.

instructions.title: Return the shrimp and serve
instructions.text: Fold the shrimp and any collected juices back into the pan and toss for 30-45 seconds, just until they are heated through and opaque all the way to the center, 145°F (63°C). Kill the heat, add the parsley, and toss once more. Serve immediately in warm bowls with the lemon wedges alongside.

tips: Buy shrimp with the shells on if you can and simmer the shells in the wine for 5 minutes before straining — it doubles the depth of the sauce for almost no work.
Do not substitute cooking wine. Use something you would actually drink, because the wine reduces down and its flaws concentrate along with its virtues.
Cold butter added off high heat is the whole trick to a mounted butter sauce. Melted butter poured in will split into a greasy slick.
Frozen shrimp are usually better than the thawed ones at the counter. Thaw them in a bowl of cold water for 15 minutes and dry them very well.
This does not hold. Have everyone at the table before the shrimp go back in the pan.
recipes.keyTemp: Shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C) — opaque, pink, and curled into a loose C. A tight O shape means they are overcooked.
recipes.pairing: The rest of the white wine you cooked with, and grilled bread rubbed with a raw garlic clove.

recipes.title: Penne alla Vodka
recipes.blurb: Tomato paste cooked down until it is sweet and brick-dark, loosened with vodka and cream into a blush sauce that clings to every ridge. The vodka is not for show — it pulls out flavors in the tomato that water and fat cannot reach.

items: 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil
2 tbsp (28 g) unsalted butter
1 small yellow onion (5 oz / 140 g), finely chopped
4 garlic cloves, minced
1/2 tsp red pepper flakes
1/3 cup (90 g) tomato paste
1/3 cup (80 ml) vodka
1 (14.5 oz / 411 g) can crushed tomatoes
3/4 cup (180 ml) heavy cream, at room temperature
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1/2 tsp black pepper
1 lb (450 g) penne rigate or rigatoni
5 qt (4.7 L) water, for the pasta
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water
2 oz (55 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated, plus more for serving
1/4 cup (10 g) fresh basil leaves, torn

instructions.title: Soften the onion
instructions.text: Heat the 2 tbsp olive oil and 2 tbsp butter in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet or wide saucepan over medium heat until the butter foams. Add the chopped onion with a pinch of salt and cook 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until it is completely soft and translucent with no crunch left. Onion that is still firm here stays firm in the finished sauce.

instructions.title: Add garlic and chili
instructions.text: Stir in the minced garlic and 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes and cook 45-60 seconds until fragrant. Keep it moving with a wooden spoon, because minced garlic has far more surface area than sliced and can go from raw to scorched in under a minute at this heat. The flakes need those few seconds in hot fat to release their color and warmth into the oil rather than sitting as dry specks in the finished sauce. The pan should smell sweet and sharp, not toasted — if you see any brown edges on the garlic, pull the pan off the burner and move straight to the tomato paste.

instructions.title: Cook the tomato paste properly
instructions.text: Add the 1/3 cup (90 g) tomato paste and stir it around the pan for 4-5 minutes over medium heat, spreading it thin against the bottom. It should darken from bright red to a deep brick color and start to stick and caramelize in patches. This step converts the raw, metallic taste of canned paste into something roasted and sweet, and it is the single biggest flavor step in the recipe.

instructions.title: Deglaze with vodka
instructions.text: Pour in the 1/3 cup (80 ml) vodka and stir hard, scraping the caramelized paste off the bottom of the pan. Let it bubble for 2-3 minutes until the harsh alcohol smell has burned off and the mixture has thickened back into a paste. Ethanol dissolves aroma compounds that are not water-soluble, which is exactly why this sauce tastes different from a plain tomato cream sauce.

instructions.title: Add the tomatoes and simmer
instructions.text: Stir in the crushed tomatoes, the 1 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper, and bring to a gentle bubble. Simmer for 12-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has thickened and darkened and a spoon dragged through leaves a track. If it spits at you, lower the heat and set a lid ajar.

instructions.title: Start the pasta
instructions.text: While the sauce simmers, bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and add the penne. Cook it 2 minutes shy of the package time — about 9 minutes for most brands — so it is firmly al dente. The ridges on penne rigate exist to grip this sauce, so use them if you can find them.

instructions.title: Temper in the cream
instructions.text: Lower the sauce to the barest simmer and stir in the 3/4 cup (180 ml) room-temperature heavy cream in a slow stream. Room-temperature cream blends smoothly, while cold cream poured into a hot acidic tomato sauce can curdle into little flecks. The sauce will turn a warm salmon pink almost instantly.

instructions.title: Let the sauce come together
instructions.text: Cook the sauce for 3-4 minutes more, barely bubbling, so the cream and tomato marry into one color and thicken slightly. Do not boil it hard once the cream is in, since a rolling boil can break dairy in an acidic sauce. Taste and adjust salt — vodka sauce usually wants more than you expect.

instructions.title: Reserve water and drain
instructions.text: Scoop out 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of pasta water, then drain the penne in a colander. Do not rinse it under the tap, however tempting — the starch on the surface is exactly what helps the sauce grip the ridges instead of sliding off into a puddle. Move fast and give the colander a shake, because penne left standing in a heap fuses together within a couple of minutes. Keep the reserved water hot next to the stove so you are always adding warm liquid to a warm pan.

instructions.title: Finish the pasta in the sauce
instructions.text: Add the drained penne to the skillet with 1/2 cup (120 ml) of pasta water and toss over medium heat for 2 minutes so the pasta absorbs sauce and the sauce tightens around it. Add more water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until it looks glossy and slightly loose, since it will thicken as it sits. Off the heat, stir in the Parmigiano and torn basil, then serve immediately with more cheese on top.

tips: Use a cheap vodka — this is one place where the expensive bottle is wasted, because you are boiling off the alcohol anyway.
The sauce alone freezes beautifully for 3 months. Freeze it before adding the cream, then stir the cream in when you reheat.
For the viral spicy pink sauce version, add 2 tbsp (30 g) of Calabrian chili paste with the tomato paste.
If the sauce ever looks broken or oily, take it off the heat and whisk in 2 tbsp (30 ml) of hot pasta water — the starch pulls it back together.
Adding 4 oz (115 g) of chopped pancetta rendered at the start turns this into a heartier weekend version worth knowing.
recipes.keyTemp: No internal temperature applies; keep the sauce at a bare simmer around 185°F (85°C) once the cream is in, and stop when a spoon dragged through the pan leaves a track that fills in slowly.
recipes.pairing: A chilled Rosato or a light Barbera, with garlic bread for the sauce left in the bowl.

recipes.title: Pesto alla Genovese with Trofie
recipes.blurb: Raw basil, pine nuts, garlic and two cheeses pounded into a bright green sauce that never sees a stove. In Liguria they cook potatoes and green beans right in the pasta water and toss it all together, and it makes the whole thing a meal.

items: 4 cups loosely packed (about 2 1/2 oz / 70 g) fresh basil leaves, stems removed
1/3 cup (45 g) pine nuts
2 garlic cloves, peeled and halved with the green germ removed
1/2 tsp coarse sea salt
2/3 cup (160 ml) mild extra-virgin olive oil (Ligurian if you can find it)
2 oz (55 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated, plus more for serving
1 oz (30 g) Pecorino Sardo or Pecorino Romano, finely grated
1 lb (450 g) trofie, trenette, or linguine
8 oz (225 g) waxy potatoes, peeled and cut into 1/2 in (1 cm) cubes
6 oz (170 g) green beans, trimmed and cut into 1 1/2 in (4 cm) lengths
5 qt (4.7 L) water
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water

instructions.title: Wash and dry the basil gently
instructions.text: Rinse the basil in cold water and dry it completely in a salad spinner or between towels, handling the leaves as little as possible. Bruised basil oxidizes and turns dark within minutes, and stray water droplets will make the pesto separate. Use only leaves — the stems are fibrous and bitter.

instructions.title: Toast the pine nuts
instructions.text: Put the 1/3 cup (45 g) pine nuts in a dry skillet over medium-low heat and shake constantly for 3-4 minutes until they are speckled gold and smell like popcorn. Tip them onto a plate immediately, because pine nuts carry enough oil to keep browning and burn in the residual heat of the pan. Let them cool completely before they go into the pesto.

instructions.title: Start with garlic and salt
instructions.text: If using a mortar, pound the halved garlic cloves with the 1/2 tsp coarse salt into a smooth paste — the salt crystals act as an abrasive that shreds the garlic. If using a food processor, pulse the garlic and salt with the pine nuts 8-10 times until finely chopped. Removing the pale green germ from the center of each clove keeps the pesto from turning acrid as it sits.

instructions.title: Add the nuts and basil
instructions.text: Add the cooled pine nuts and work them into a paste, then add the basil in three handfuls. In a mortar, use a grinding, circular motion against the wall rather than pounding straight down; in a processor, pulse in short bursts and scrape the sides between them. Long continuous blending heats the basil and turns it bitter and army-green.

instructions.title: Stream in the oil
instructions.text: With the processor running on low, or while stirring the mortar, pour in the 2/3 cup (160 ml) olive oil in a thin steady stream until the pesto is a loose, spoonable paste. A gentle mild oil is traditional here — a fiercely peppery Tuscan oil will bully the basil. Stop as soon as it comes together.

instructions.title: Fold in the cheeses by hand
instructions.text: Transfer the pesto to a bowl and stir in the Parmigiano and Pecorino with a spoon rather than the machine. Blade-blended cheese gets pasty and can turn gluey. Taste and add salt only if needed, remembering the pasta water will bring more.

instructions.title: Boil the potatoes first
instructions.text: Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and add the cubed potatoes. Boil for 5 minutes; they need a head start because they take longer than the pasta. The starch they release also makes the water even better for building the sauce later.

instructions.title: Add pasta and green beans
instructions.text: Add the pasta and the green beans to the same pot with the potatoes. Cook until the pasta is 1 minute shy of the package time — trofie takes 7-8 minutes, dried linguine about 9. Everything finishes together, which is the whole elegance of the Ligurian method.

instructions.title: Loosen the pesto with pasta water
instructions.text: Scoop 1 cup (240 ml) of the starchy water and whisk about 1/3 cup (80 ml) of it into the bowl of pesto until it loosens into a pourable sauce. Doing this in the bowl, off the heat, prevents the cheese from seizing and the basil from cooking. The pesto should thin to about the consistency of heavy cream.

instructions.title: Toss everything off the heat
instructions.text: Drain the pasta and vegetables and add them to the pesto bowl, then toss hard for 30-45 seconds, adding more pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until everything is evenly coated and glossy. Never return pesto to a hot burner — heat dulls the green to olive and kills the raw perfume that makes it worth making. Serve immediately with extra Parmigiano.

tips: Freeze pesto in an ice cube tray without the cheese, then bag the cubes. Stir in the grated cheese after thawing and it tastes almost freshly made for up to 3 months.
To keep leftover pesto green in the fridge, press it into a jar and pour a 1/4 in (6 mm) layer of olive oil over the top to block air. It keeps 5 days.
Walnuts stand in for pine nuts at a fraction of the price and are traditional in parts of Liguria. Use 1/2 cup (55 g) and toast them the same way.
Blanching the basil for 10 seconds and shocking it in ice water locks in a brilliant green forever, at the cost of a little fresh aroma. Good trick when you want it to look perfect.
Trofie and trenette are the classic shapes because their twists and edges catch the pesto, but any short twisted pasta like fusilli or casarecce works well.
recipes.keyTemp: No cooking temperature applies to the sauce — pesto must stay raw. Toss it off the heat and keep it under about 140°F (60°C) or the basil darkens and the cheese goes grainy.
recipes.pairing: A cold Ligurian Vermentino or Pigato, and a plate of sliced ripe tomatoes with salt.

recipes.title: Linguine alle Vongole
recipes.blurb: Clams steamed open in white wine and garlic, their briny juice reduced into a sauce that tastes like the sea in the best way. Nothing but pasta water and starch binds it, and it comes together in the time it takes to boil linguine.

items: 2 lb (900 g) littleneck or Manila clams, in the shell
1/3 cup (80 g) kosher salt dissolved in 4 qt (3.8 L) cold water, for purging the clams
1 lb (450 g) linguine
5 qt (4.7 L) water, for the pasta
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water
1/3 cup (80 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for finishing
6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1/2 tsp red pepper flakes
3/4 cup (180 ml) dry white wine such as Vermentino
1/3 cup (13 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1 tbsp (15 ml) fresh lemon juice
1/2 tsp black pepper

instructions.title: Purge the clams
instructions.text: Dissolve the 1/3 cup (80 g) kosher salt in 4 qt (3.8 L) of cold water — roughly the salinity of seawater — and submerge the clams for 1 hour in the refrigerator. Water any fresher than this kills them instead of relaxing them, which is why plain tap water is the classic mistake. Salt water at the right strength tricks them into breathing normally and spitting out the sand trapped inside, and you will see grit on the bottom of the bowl afterward. Lift the clams out with your hands rather than pouring, so the sand stays behind.

instructions.title: Sort out the dead ones
instructions.text: Scrub the shells under cold running water and inspect each clam. Any that are cracked, or that stay wide open after you tap them firmly on the counter, are dead and must go in the trash. A live clam clamps shut within about 10 seconds of being tapped — this check is not optional with shellfish.

instructions.title: Get everything ready
instructions.text: Slice the garlic, chop the parsley, and set the wine, oil and a lid for your skillet within arm's reach. Once the clams start opening, the window between perfect and rubbery is about 90 seconds. This dish rewards a fully prepped counter more than almost anything else in the chapter.

instructions.title: Boil the water
instructions.text: Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a rolling boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt. Salt a little lighter than usual because the clam liquor is genuinely salty and will season the finished sauce all on its own — over-salt here and there is no way to walk it back. Do not start the pasta yet; the clams and the linguine need to go in at the same moment so they finish together. Get the pot to a full boil and then just hold it there while you work on the clams.

instructions.title: Infuse the oil
instructions.text: Heat the 1/3 cup (80 ml) olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet with a lid over medium heat, add the sliced garlic and 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes, and cook 2 minutes until the garlic is pale gold at the edges. Adjust the heat so the garlic barely bubbles rather than fries. Burnt garlic here poisons the whole delicate flavor of the clams.

instructions.title: Steam the clams open
instructions.text: Add the clams and the 3/4 cup (180 ml) white wine, raise the heat to medium-high, and clamp the lid on. Steam for 5-8 minutes, shaking the pan once or twice, until most shells have opened. Lift each clam out with tongs the moment it opens rather than waiting for the last stubborn one — clams left in the pan for an extra 3 minutes turn into pencil erasers.

instructions.title: Cook the linguine
instructions.text: Drop the linguine into the boiling water as soon as the clams go in the skillet. Cook 2 minutes less than the package time, about 8 minutes, so it is stiffly al dente. It has two more minutes of cooking to do in the clam broth.

instructions.title: Reduce and strain the broth
instructions.text: Discard any clams that stayed shut after 8 minutes of steaming. If the broth looks sandy, pour it through a fine sieve lined with a paper towel and return it to the pan, then simmer 2-3 minutes to reduce it slightly and concentrate the flavor. You should have roughly 1 cup (240 ml) of intensely savory liquid.

instructions.title: Shell some of the clams
instructions.text: Pull the meat out of about half the clams and leave the rest in their shells for looks. This way every forkful actually gets clam meat instead of you chasing shells around the bowl. Keep the shelled meat with the reserved whole clams under a plate so they stay warm.

instructions.title: Finish the pasta in the broth
instructions.text: Reserve 1 cup (240 ml) of pasta water, drain the linguine, and add it straight to the skillet of broth over medium heat. Toss constantly for 2 minutes, adding pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time, until the liquid turns slightly creamy and clings to the strands. That cloudiness is the starch emulsifying the oil and clam juice into a real sauce.

instructions.title: Bring the clams back and serve
instructions.text: Turn off the heat, add all the clams and their meat, the parsley, lemon juice and black pepper, and toss for 30 seconds just to warm them through. Finish with a thin drizzle of raw olive oil for aroma. Serve immediately with an empty bowl on the table for shells, and no cheese — cheese on clams is a genuine offense in Italy.

tips: Buy clams the day you cook them and keep them in the fridge in an open bowl covered with a damp towel, never sealed in a plastic bag or sitting in fresh water, which suffocates them.
Manila clams are smaller, sweeter and open faster; littlenecks are meatier. Either works, but do not mix sizes in one pan since they open at different rates.
If your clams still taste gritty, next time purge them for a full 2 hours and change the salt water once halfway through.
Canned clams are a reasonable pantry backup: use two 6.5 oz (184 g) cans with their juice, add them at the very end, and simmer just 1 minute.
Vongole in bianco is the version here. For rosso, add 1 cup (150 g) of halved cherry tomatoes with the wine and cook them down until they collapse.
recipes.keyTemp: Clams are done the instant their shells open, around 145°F (63°C) internally. Discard any that refuse to open after 8 minutes of steaming.
recipes.pairing: The same crisp Vermentino you cooked with, and grilled bread for the broth at the bottom of the bowl.

recipes.title: Baked Mac and Cheese with Bechamel
recipes.blurb: A real flour-and-butter bechamel means this sauce stays creamy in the oven instead of turning oily and grainy. Sharp cheddar for flavor, Gruyere for melt, and a buttered panko lid that shatters when your fork goes in.

items: 1 lb (450 g) elbow macaroni or cavatappi
5 qt (4.7 L) water
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water
1 tbsp (14 g) unsalted butter, for tossing the drained pasta
5 tbsp (70 g) unsalted butter
1/3 cup (42 g) all-purpose flour
4 cups (960 ml) whole milk, warmed to about 110°F (43°C)
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt
1 tsp mustard powder
1/2 tsp onion powder
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
1/4 tsp cayenne pepper
12 oz (340 g) sharp cheddar, shredded from a block
4 oz (115 g) Gruyere, shredded from a block
1 1/2 cups (75 g) panko breadcrumbs
3 tbsp (42 g) unsalted butter, melted
1 oz (30 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated
1/4 tsp sweet paprika

instructions.title: Shred your own cheese
instructions.text: Grate all 16 oz (455 g) of cheddar and Gruyere from blocks on the large holes of a box grater and let it sit at room temperature while you work. Bagged shredded cheese is dusted with potato starch and cellulose to stop clumping, and that same coating stops it from melting smoothly into a sauce. Room-temperature cheese also melts without shocking the bechamel.

instructions.title: Heat the oven
instructions.text: Set a rack in the upper third of the oven and heat it to 375°F (190°C). Butter a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish or a 3 qt (3 L) casserole. The high rack position puts the crumb topping close to the heat so it browns while the inside stays creamy.

instructions.title: Undercook the macaroni
instructions.text: Boil 5 qt (4.7 L) of water with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and cook the pasta for only 5-6 minutes, roughly 3 minutes shy of the package time. It should still be chalky in the center. It will absorb sauce and finish cooking in the oven, and fully cooked pasta here turns to mush.

instructions.title: Drain but do not rinse
instructions.text: Drain the pasta and toss it with 1 tbsp (14 g) of butter so it does not fuse into a block while you make the sauce. Skip rinsing — the starch clinging to the surface helps the cheese sauce grab hold. Spread it out in the colander so it stops cooking.

instructions.title: Make the roux
instructions.text: Melt the 5 tbsp (70 g) butter in a large saucepan over medium heat, then whisk in the 1/3 cup (42 g) flour and cook for 2 minutes, whisking constantly. It should bubble like wet sand and smell faintly nutty, but stay pale blond — this is a white roux and browning it would cost you thickening power. Two minutes is the minimum to cook out the raw flour taste.

instructions.title: Build the bechamel
instructions.text: Pour in the warm milk in three additions, whisking hard after each one until completely smooth before adding the next. Adding it all at once is how you get lumps, and warm milk incorporates far more easily than cold. Once all the milk is in, the mixture will look alarmingly thin, which is normal.

instructions.title: Cook it to nappe
instructions.text: Bring the sauce to a bare simmer over medium heat, whisking often, and cook 6-8 minutes until it thickly coats the back of a spoon and holds a clean line when you draw a finger through it. It should read about 185°F (85°C). Stir in the salt, mustard powder, onion powder, nutmeg and cayenne now, while it is still just sauce.

instructions.title: Melt in the cheese off the heat
instructions.text: Take the pan completely off the burner and wait 1 minute, then add the cheddar and Gruyere in four handfuls, whisking each one in fully before the next. Direct heat above roughly 175°F (79°C) makes cheese proteins tighten and squeeze out fat, which is exactly what a grainy, greasy mac and cheese looks like. Reserve 4 oz (115 g) of the cheddar for the top if you want extra pull.

instructions.title: Combine and taste
instructions.text: Fold the drained macaroni into the cheese sauce until every piece is coated. The mixture should look almost soupy — noticeably looser than you want the final dish — because the pasta will drink up a lot of it in the oven. Taste for salt now, since the topping will not fix an underseasoned base.

instructions.title: Make the crumb topping
instructions.text: Toss the 1 1/2 cups (75 g) panko with the 3 tbsp melted butter, the grated Parmigiano and the paprika until every crumb is lightly slicked. Buttered crumbs brown evenly and stay crisp; dry crumbs scorch in patches and taste like sawdust. Scatter them over the top in an even layer.

instructions.title: Bake until bubbling and gold
instructions.text: Bake for 25-30 minutes, until the topping is deep golden and the sauce is bubbling up around the edges and the center reads 165°F (74°C). If the crumbs brown before the center is hot, tent loosely with foil. Let it rest 10 minutes so the sauce sets enough to serve in scoops.

tips: Never let cheese sauce boil after the cheese is in. If it looks broken, whisk in 2 tbsp (30 ml) of warm milk off the heat and it will usually come back together.

Cheese blend matters more than any single cheese: sharp cheddar brings the flavor but melts stringy, while Gruyere, fontina, or young Gouda bring the silk. Aim for roughly 3 parts flavor cheese to 1 part melter.
Assemble it up to 24 hours ahead without the crumbs, refrigerate, then add the topping and bake from cold for 40-45 minutes covered plus 15 uncovered.
For a stovetop version, stop after folding the pasta into the sauce and serve immediately — it is looser, faster, and honestly just as good.
A teaspoon of mustard powder is not there to taste like mustard. The acid sharpens the cheese and keeps the sauce from tasting flat and heavy.
recipes.keyTemp: Melt the cheese off the heat below about 175°F (79°C) so it does not break, and bake until the center of the dish reaches 165°F (74°C).
recipes.pairing: A cold hard cider or a hoppy pale ale, with something sharp on the side like quick-pickled onions or a vinegary slaw.
