recipes.title: Stuffed Shells with Ricotta and Spinach
recipes.blurb: Big pasta shells filled with herby ricotta and spinach, nestled into marinara and baked until the tops go golden. It is fussy in the nicest way, and it is the kind of thing you can build ahead and slide into the oven when people arrive.

items: 12 oz (340 g) jumbo pasta shells (about 36 shells; you will fill 24)
5 qt (4.7 L) water
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water
4 cups (960 ml) marinara sauce, homemade or a good jarred brand
1 tbsp (15 ml) olive oil
1 1/2 lb (680 g) whole-milk ricotta, drained if watery
10 oz (285 g) frozen chopped spinach, thawed and squeezed very dry
1 large egg, lightly beaten
4 oz (115 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated, plus more for the table
8 oz (225 g) low-moisture whole-milk mozzarella, shredded, divided
1/4 cup (10 g) chopped fresh basil, plus a few whole leaves for serving
2 tbsp (8 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1 1/4 tsp kosher salt
1/2 tsp black pepper
1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
2 garlic cloves, finely minced

instructions.title: Drain the ricotta
instructions.text: If your ricotta looks wet or has liquid pooled on top, spoon it into a fine sieve set over a bowl and let it drain for 20 minutes. Excess whey turns the filling loose and it will weep out into the sauce during baking, leaving you with watery shells. Good drained ricotta should mound on a spoon and hold its shape.

instructions.title: Squeeze the spinach bone dry
instructions.text: Wrap the thawed spinach in a clean kitchen towel and wring it out over the sink with real force. You should get about 1/2 cup (120 ml) of green water out of a 10 oz package, and the spinach should end up as a dense, dry puck. Any water you leave behind ends up in the filling.

instructions.title: Heat the oven
instructions.text: Set a rack in the middle of the oven and heat it to 375°F (190°C). Spread the 1 tbsp olive oil and 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of the marinara across the bottom of a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish. That layer of sauce keeps the shells from sticking and gently steams them from below.

instructions.title: Boil the shells carefully
instructions.text: Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and add the shells, stirring gently so they do not nest inside each other. Cook 3 minutes less than the package time — usually about 8 minutes — so they are pliable but still firm. Overcooked shells tear the second you try to fill them.

instructions.title: Cool the shells flat
instructions.text: Drain the shells and lay them in a single layer on a lightly oiled sheet pan, open side up, and let them cool for 5-10 minutes until you can handle them. Piling them in a colander glues them together and you will rip half of them apart. Discard any that split during boiling — that is why you cooked extra.

instructions.title: Mix the filling
instructions.text: In a large bowl, stir the drained ricotta with the squeezed spinach, the beaten egg, three-quarters of the Parmigiano, half the mozzarella, the basil, parsley, garlic, 1 1/4 tsp salt, pepper and nutmeg. Mix until uniform but do not overwork it. The egg binds the filling so it sets into creamy pockets instead of running out into the sauce.

instructions.title: Taste and adjust
instructions.text: Taste the filling now — it is safe apart from the raw egg, so take a small spoonful and check the seasoning. Ricotta is bland and soaks up salt, so it usually needs more than seems right. It should taste slightly over-seasoned on its own, since the pasta and sauce will mute it.

instructions.title: Fill the shells
instructions.text: Spoon the filling into a zip-top bag, snip 3/4 in (2 cm) off one corner, and pipe about 3 tbsp (45 g) into each shell. That is the amount that fills a jumbo shell to the rim without bulging, and it works out so that 24 shells use the bowl of filling almost exactly — if you are running ahead or behind, adjust on the next few. A bag is dramatically faster and neater than a spoon, and it packs the filling in without splitting the pasta. Do not overstuff, or the filling pushes out and scorches on the pan as it heats and expands.

instructions.title: Nestle them in the sauce
instructions.text: Arrange the filled shells open side up in the sauced dish in neat rows, packed snugly against each other so they support one another. Twenty-four shells fit a 9x13 in dish almost exactly. Spoon the remaining 2 1/2 cups (600 ml) of marinara over and between them, leaving the very tops of the filling exposed.

instructions.title: Top and bake covered
instructions.text: Scatter the remaining mozzarella and Parmigiano over the top, then cover the dish tightly with foil, tenting it so it does not touch the cheese. Bake for 30 minutes covered — the trapped steam finishes cooking the pasta and heats the filling through without drying the exposed edges. You should hear it bubbling when you pull it out.

instructions.title: Uncover and brown
instructions.text: Remove the foil and bake another 15-20 minutes, until the cheese is melted with golden brown spots and the center of a middle shell reads 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer. That temperature also confirms the egg in the filling is fully cooked. If it is hot but pale, broil for 90 seconds while watching it constantly.

instructions.title: Rest and serve
instructions.text: Let the dish sit for 10 minutes before serving so the filling firms up and the sauce stops running. Serve 4 shells per person with a spoonful of sauce from the bottom of the pan. Finish with torn basil and more grated Parmigiano at the table.

tips: Assemble the whole dish up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate covered. Bake straight from the fridge, adding 15 minutes to the covered time.
To freeze, assemble in a foil pan and freeze unbaked up to 3 months. Bake from frozen, covered, at 375°F (190°C) for 70 minutes, then uncovered for 20.
Fresh spinach works too: wilt 1 lb (450 g) in a dry pan, cool it, then chop and squeeze it as hard as you would the frozen kind.
Ricotta quality is the whole dish. Look for one with a short ingredient list and no gums; supermarket ricotta with stabilizers stays chalky no matter what you do.
For a meaty version, brown 8 oz (225 g) of Italian sausage and stir it into the marinara rather than the filling, so the ricotta stays light.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake until the center of a middle shell registers 165°F (74°C), which both heats the dish through and fully cooks the egg in the ricotta filling.
recipes.pairing: A medium-bodied Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and garlic bread, with a lemony arugula salad to finish.

recipes.title: Pasta Primavera
recipes.blurb: Spring vegetables cooked in stages so each one keeps its own texture, tossed with butter, Parmigiano and lemon into a light sauce built on pasta water. It is bright and green and does not feel like a compromise.

items: 8 oz (225 g) asparagus, woody ends snapped off, cut into 1 1/2 in (4 cm) pieces
6 oz (170 g) sugar snap peas, strings pulled
1 medium zucchini (8 oz / 225 g), halved lengthwise and sliced 1/4 in (6 mm) thick
1 cup (140 g) frozen peas, thawed
1 pint (10 oz / 285 g) cherry tomatoes, halved
1 small shallot (1 oz / 30 g), thinly sliced
3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
12 oz (340 g) farfalle, fusilli, or penne
5 qt (4.7 L) water
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water
3 tbsp (45 ml) olive oil
4 tbsp (55 g) unsalted butter, cold, cut into 4 pieces
1/3 cup (80 ml) heavy cream
3 oz (85 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated, plus more for serving
1 tbsp (15 ml) fresh lemon juice plus 1 tsp finely grated zest
1/4 cup (10 g) chopped fresh basil, plus a few whole leaves for serving, and 2 tbsp (8 g) chopped mint
1 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp black pepper

instructions.title: Cut everything to the same size
instructions.text: Prep all the vegetables before you turn on a burner and aim for pieces around 1 1/2 in (4 cm) or a comparable bite. Primavera falls apart when half the vegetables are baby-sized and half are chunks, because they cook at wildly different rates. Keep each type in its own pile since they go into the pan separately.

instructions.title: Set up an ice bath
instructions.text: Fill a large bowl with cold water and a few handfuls of ice and set it next to the stove. Blanched green vegetables keep cooking on their own heat and turn drab olive within a minute or two unless you stop them cold. This is the single step that keeps primavera looking like spring.

instructions.title: Blanch the asparagus and snap peas
instructions.text: Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt. Drop in the asparagus for 90 seconds and the snap peas for 60 seconds — cook them separately so you can time each — then lift them out with a spider straight into the ice bath. They should be bright green and still audibly crisp when you bite one.

instructions.title: Dry the blanched vegetables
instructions.text: Scoop the chilled vegetables out of the ice bath after 2 minutes and spread them on a towel to drain. Wet vegetables will thin your sauce and stop the zucchini from browning later. Keep the blanching water boiling — you are cooking the pasta in it.

instructions.title: Brown the zucchini
instructions.text: Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then add the zucchini in a single layer with a pinch of salt. Cook 3-4 minutes without stirring much until the cut sides are golden, then flip and cook 1 minute more. Zucchini holds a lot of water, so crowding the pan turns it to mush — do it in two batches if you must.

instructions.title: Cook the aromatics and tomatoes
instructions.text: Move the zucchini to a plate, add the last 1 tbsp oil to the pan, and cook the sliced shallot for 2 minutes until soft. Add the garlic for 45 seconds, then the halved cherry tomatoes with 1/2 tsp salt and cook 3-4 minutes until they slump and release their juice. Press a few against the pan with a spoon to help them break down into the base of the sauce.

instructions.title: Cook the pasta al dente
instructions.text: Add the pasta to the still-boiling salted water — the same water you blanched the greens in, which is now faintly vegetal and all the better for it — and cook 1 minute less than the package time, about 9 minutes for farfalle. Stir for the first 30 seconds so the pieces do not stick to each other or to the bottom. Farfalle is worth watching because the pinched center stays firm longer than the wings, so bite the middle of one to judge it. It gets a final minute in the pan with the sauce, which is where it finishes.

instructions.title: Reserve the water
instructions.text: Scoop out 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of pasta water before draining, then drain the pasta without rinsing it. This water is doing double duty here: it thins the cream to a coating consistency and its starch binds the cold butter into a sauce that clings rather than pooling. Because you cooked vegetables in this pot too, it carries a little of their flavor as well. Keep it hot beside the pan, since cold liquid dropped into a butter emulsion will split it in seconds.

instructions.title: Build the sauce
instructions.text: Add the 1/3 cup (80 ml) cream and 1/2 cup (120 ml) pasta water to the tomato pan and bring it to a gentle simmer for 1-2 minutes. Turn the heat to low and swirl in the cold butter one piece at a time until the sauce looks glossy and slightly thickened. Cold butter added slowly over low heat emulsifies; melted butter dumped in splits.

instructions.title: Bring everything together
instructions.text: Add the drained pasta, the blanched asparagus and snap peas, the browned zucchini, and the thawed peas to the pan and toss over medium heat for 1-2 minutes. Add pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until everything is lightly coated and the sauce clings rather than pools. The vegetables only need to warm through, not cook further.

instructions.title: Finish off the heat
instructions.text: Take the pan off the burner, then add the Parmigiano, lemon juice and zest, basil, mint, and the remaining salt and pepper, tossing until the cheese melts into the sauce. Adding cheese off the heat keeps it creamy instead of stringy, and the lemon added last stays bright. Taste and adjust — this dish needs more salt and acid than you expect.

instructions.title: Serve right away
instructions.text: Divide among four warm bowls and top with a little extra Parmigiano and a few torn basil leaves. Primavera is best in the first five minutes, while the greens still snap and the sauce is loose. If it tightens up on the way to the table, loosen it with a splash of the reserved water.

tips: Cook the vegetables in stages rather than dumping them all in at once. Staggering is the entire technique here and it is what separates this from a sad pile of steamed vegetables.
Swap freely with the season: broccolini, green beans, leeks, fennel, or corn all work. Just keep the rule of blanching the green things and browning the watery things.
For a dairy-free version, skip the cream and cheese and build the sauce with 1/4 cup (60 ml) olive oil, the lemon, and an extra 1/2 cup (120 ml) pasta water.
Blanch the greens up to a day ahead and refrigerate them dry in a container. It cuts the active cooking down to about 15 minutes on a weeknight.
A pinch of red pepper flakes with the garlic gives the whole dish a lift without making it spicy.
recipes.keyTemp: No internal temperature applies. The cue is the vegetables: bright green and crisp-tender, meaning a piece of asparagus bends slightly but snaps back rather than drooping. Keep the finished sauce below 175°F (79°C) so the cheese stays smooth.
recipes.pairing: A cold Sauvignon Blanc or a dry rose, and crusty bread with good butter.

recipes.title: Cajun Chicken Pasta
recipes.blurb: Blackened chicken sliced over penne in a peppery cream sauce built on the browned bits left in the pan. It is the dish that makes a Tuesday feel like a night out, and the whole thing is done in forty minutes.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) boneless skinless chicken breasts, halved horizontally into 4 cutlets
2 tbsp (18 g) Cajun seasoning, divided
1/2 tsp kosher salt (omit if your Cajun blend is salt-heavy)
2 tbsp (30 ml) neutral oil such as canola
2 tbsp (28 g) unsalted butter
1 red bell pepper (6 oz / 170 g), sliced 1/4 in (6 mm) thick
1 green bell pepper (6 oz / 170 g), sliced 1/4 in (6 mm) thick
1/2 medium red onion (4 oz / 115 g), sliced thin
4 garlic cloves, minced
1/2 cup (120 ml) low-sodium chicken stock
1 1/2 cups (360 ml) heavy cream
1 cup (150 g) cherry tomatoes, halved
3 oz (85 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated, plus more for serving
3 scallions, thinly sliced
12 oz (340 g) penne or fettuccine
5 qt (4.7 L) water
2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt, for the pasta water

instructions.title: Butterfly the chicken
instructions.text: Lay each breast flat, rest your palm on top, and slice horizontally through the middle to make two thin cutlets about 1/2 in (1 cm) thick. Thin, even cutlets cook in 3-4 minutes a side and stay juicy, while a whole thick breast dries out at the edges before the center is safe. You should end up with 4 cutlets of roughly the same thickness.

instructions.title: Season and rest
instructions.text: Pat the cutlets very dry and rub them all over with 1 1/2 tbsp of the Cajun seasoning and the 1/2 tsp salt. Let them sit at room temperature for 10 minutes while you prep the vegetables — this takes the fridge chill off so they cook evenly. Dry surfaces are what let the spices form a dark crust instead of a paste.

instructions.title: Get the pan hot
instructions.text: Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) cast iron or heavy stainless skillet over medium-high for 2 minutes until the oil shimmers and moves like water. Cast iron holds heat well enough to blacken the spice crust properly. If it starts smoking hard, pull the pan off for 20 seconds — Cajun spice blends contain paprika and garlic powder that scorch bitter.

instructions.title: Blacken the chicken
instructions.text: Lay the cutlets in the pan without crowding, working in two batches if needed, and cook 3-4 minutes per side without moving them. You want a dark mahogany crust and, more importantly, an instant-read thermometer reading of 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point of every cutlet — poultry is not safe below that, and a 1/2 in cutlet carries over only a degree or two off the heat, so do not pull it early and hope. If a piece is browned but reads low, give it another 30-60 seconds a side rather than turning the heat up. Move them to a cutting board and let them rest 5 minutes so the juices redistribute instead of running out when you slice.

instructions.title: Start the pasta
instructions.text: Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and add the 12 oz (340 g) of penne. Cook it 1 to 2 minutes less than the package time, usually about 9 minutes, so it is firmly al dente with a chalky center. Time it to come out while the chicken is resting, so nothing sits around going cold. It finishes in the cream sauce, where it will drink up a good part of the liquid and the Cajun seasoning along with it.

instructions.title: Cook the peppers
instructions.text: Lower the skillet to medium, add the 2 tbsp butter, and cook the sliced bell peppers and red onion for 5-6 minutes until they soften and pick up a few charred edges. Stir occasionally, scraping the fond from the chicken up as you go. You want them tender but with a little bite left, not limp.

instructions.title: Add the garlic
instructions.text: Stir in the minced garlic and the remaining 1/2 tbsp of Cajun seasoning and cook 45 seconds until it smells fragrant. Toasting the spice in fat blooms the paprika and dried herbs and rounds out their flavor. Do not let the garlic take on color.

instructions.title: Deglaze the pan
instructions.text: Pour in the 1/2 cup (120 ml) chicken stock and scrape the bottom of the skillet hard with a wooden spoon until every browned bit lifts. Those bits are pure concentrated chicken flavor and they are the entire reason this sauce tastes like more than cream. Simmer 2 minutes until reduced by about half.

instructions.title: Build the cream sauce
instructions.text: Add the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) heavy cream and the halved cherry tomatoes, then bring to a gentle simmer and cook 4-5 minutes, stirring often. The sauce should reduce enough to coat the back of a spoon and hold a line when you swipe a finger through it. Keep it at a lazy bubble; a hard boil can break the cream.

instructions.title: Reserve water and add the pasta
instructions.text: Scoop out 1 cup (240 ml) of pasta water, drain the pasta, and add it straight to the skillet. Toss over medium heat for 1-2 minutes so the noodles absorb some sauce and thicken it. Add pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time if it gets too tight.

instructions.title: Finish with cheese off the heat
instructions.text: Pull the pan off the burner, add the grated Parmigiano, and toss until it melts smoothly into the sauce. Cheese added to a simmering pan goes stringy and grainy, while cheese added to a pan off the heat turns silky. Taste for salt — Cajun blends vary enormously in how salty they are.

instructions.title: Slice, top, and serve
instructions.text: Slice the rested chicken against the grain into 1/2 in (1 cm) strips and lay them over the pasta rather than stirring them in, so the crust stays crisp. Scatter the sliced scallions over the top. Serve immediately with extra Parmigiano at the table.

tips: Make your own Cajun blend: 2 tsp paprika, 1 tsp each garlic powder, onion powder and dried oregano, 1/2 tsp each cayenne, black pepper, thyme and salt. You control the heat and the salt.
Chicken thighs are more forgiving than breasts and hard to dry out. Use 1 1/2 lb (680 g) boneless thighs and cook them to 175°F (79°C) for the best texture.
Half-and-half will not hold up here. The acid from the tomatoes plus the reduction needs the fat in heavy cream or it will curdle.
Let the chicken rest the full 5 minutes before slicing. Cut it straight out of the pan and you will lose a puddle of juice to the cutting board.
Leftovers reheat surprisingly well in a skillet over low heat with a splash of milk or stock to loosen the sauce.
recipes.keyTemp: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer at the thickest part of the cutlet — check every piece, since thin cutlets vary and carryover in a 1/2 in cutlet is only a degree or two, not enough to close a gap. Rest the cooked cutlets 5 minutes before slicing so the juices redistribute.
recipes.pairing: A cold lager or a lightly oaked Chardonnay, with cornbread or a simple slaw on the side.

recipes.title: Brown Butter and Sage Ravioli
recipes.blurb: Butter cooked until its milk solids toast to hazelnut brown, crisp sage leaves, a squeeze of lemon, and good ravioli. Four ingredients and fifteen minutes, and it tastes like something you would pay thirty dollars for.

items: 1 lb (450 g) fresh cheese or butternut squash ravioli
4 qt (3.8 L) water
1 tbsp (18 g) fine sea salt, for the pasta water
8 tbsp (113 g / 1 stick) unsalted butter, cut into 8 even pieces
1 tbsp (14 g) cold unsalted butter, held back to stop the browning if it races ahead
20 fresh sage leaves
1/3 cup (40 g) walnuts, roughly chopped, optional
2 tsp (10 ml) fresh lemon juice
2 oz (55 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano, finely grated
1/4 tsp flaky sea salt and 1/4 tsp black pepper, for finishing
1/8 tsp freshly grated nutmeg

instructions.title: Use a light-colored pan
instructions.text: Choose a stainless steel or light-enameled 10-12 in (25-30 cm) skillet rather than dark nonstick or cast iron. Brown butter is judged entirely by color, and in a dark pan you cannot see the milk solids change until they have already burned. This one choice makes the difference between nutty and acrid.

instructions.title: Get the water going first
instructions.text: Bring 4 qt (3.8 L) of water to a gentle boil with 1 tbsp (18 g) fine sea salt. Do not let it hit a violent rolling boil — fresh ravioli are fragile and hard boiling tears them open, spilling the filling into the pot. You want a lively simmer with bubbles breaking steadily across the surface.

instructions.title: Melt the butter
instructions.text: Set the skillet over medium heat and add all 8 tbsp (113 g) of butter at once, swirling the pan as it melts. Cutting it into even pieces means it melts at the same rate rather than some browning before the rest has liquefied. Once melted it will foam up loudly as the water in the butter boils off.

instructions.title: Cook through the foam
instructions.text: Keep swirling the pan every 15-20 seconds and let the butter foam and crackle for 2-3 minutes. That noise is water evaporating, and when it goes quiet you are close to the browning stage. Do not walk away at any point during this step.

instructions.title: Watch for the brown flecks
instructions.text: After 4-6 minutes total the foam will subside, the butter will turn a clear amber, and specks of milk solid will appear on the bottom of the pan. Tilt the skillet and look: when those specks are the color of toasted hazelnuts and the whole kitchen smells nutty and sweet, you are done. Butter goes from perfect to burnt in about 20 seconds, so be ready to move.

instructions.title: Fry the sage
instructions.text: Drop the 20 sage leaves and the walnuts if using into the hot butter and let them sizzle for 30-45 seconds. The leaves will curl, go a shade darker, and turn crisp like potato chips. Fish them out with a slotted spoon onto a paper towel and sprinkle with a pinch of salt — they are the garnish and half the pleasure of the dish.

instructions.title: Stop the butter cooking
instructions.text: Immediately pull the skillet off the heat and set it on a cool burner or a folded towel. The pan holds enough heat to keep browning the butter well past where you want it. If it looks like it is racing ahead, drop in the reserved 1 tbsp (14 g) of cold butter to bring the temperature down fast.

instructions.title: Cook the ravioli gently
instructions.text: Slide the ravioli into the simmering water in batches so they are not crowded and stir once, very gently, with a slotted spoon. They are done 2-4 minutes after they float to the surface, when the pasta at the sealed edges is tender to the bite. Overcooked ravioli split and dump their filling, so start tasting early.

instructions.title: Save some pasta water
instructions.text: Scoop out 3/4 cup (180 ml) of the starchy water before you lift the ravioli out. Brown butter alone is pure fat and will slide right off the pasta — the starch in this water is what turns it into a sauce that clings. Keep it right beside the pan.

instructions.title: Emulsify the sauce
instructions.text: Return the skillet to low heat, add 1/3 cup (80 ml) of the pasta water, and swirl vigorously for about 30 seconds until the butter and water come together into a slightly thickened, cloudy sauce. Stir in the 2 tsp lemon juice and the nutmeg. The lemon cuts the richness and keeps the whole thing from feeling heavy.

instructions.title: Coat and serve
instructions.text: Lift the ravioli straight from the pot into the skillet with a slotted spoon and toss gently for 30 seconds, adding a splash more pasta water if the sauce looks tight. Spoon them onto warm plates, scatter the crisp sage and walnuts over the top, and finish with the Parmigiano, flaky salt and black pepper. Serve at once, while the sage is still crisp.

tips: Brown butter keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge and freezes for 3 months. Make a double batch and you are ten minutes from dinner any night.
Butternut squash or mushroom ravioli are the classic partners, but a good cheese ravioli with the nutmeg and lemon is just as strong.
If you burn the butter, throw it out and start over. Burnt milk solids taste bitter and there is no ingredient that hides it.
Fresh sage is essential; dried sage turns to dust in hot butter and tastes musty. If you cannot find it, use 10 fresh thyme sprigs instead.
Toasting the walnuts in the butter for the full 45 seconds does double duty — it crisps the nuts and leaves a faint toasted flavor behind in the sauce.
recipes.keyTemp: Butter browns at about 250°F (120°C) once the water has cooked off; pull it the moment the milk solids turn hazelnut brown, because past roughly 300°F (150°C) they burn bitter within seconds.
recipes.pairing: A glass of Pinot Noir or a dry Riesling, with a bitter salad of radicchio and toasted hazelnuts.
